name: Venkatesh
definition: Venkatesh is a composite portrait of a tomato commission agent in his late thirties working in Bangarpet market, Kolar district, one of Karnataka's major tomato trading centres. He navigates the daily volatility of farm-gate prices, coordinates lorry loads to Bengaluru and beyond, and balances brokerage income against the pressures of advancing credit to farmers and absorbing crop-glut losses.

topics.label: Daily Life and Work
topics.profile: Venkatesh begins his day before dawn at the Bangarpet tomato market yard, where lorries arrive from surrounding villages—Srinivaspur, Malur, and even from across the Andhra border. He brokers deals between growers and wholesale buyers, charging a 7-8 per cent commission on each transaction. During the peak harvest months from December to March, he can handle fifteen to twenty tonnes a day; in the lean season, turnover falls to a trickle and his income shrinks. The work is entirely cash-based and recorded in dog-eared ledgers. Price swings are brutal: a crate fetching ₹600 one week may crash to ₹80 the next, wiping out both the farmer's margin and his own advance. He owns no land himself but rents a small godown near the yard and employs two daily-wage loaders. His phone never stops ringing—buyers in Bengaluru, transporters on the highway, farmers asking for credit. By mid-morning the floor is slick with crushed tomatoes; by noon the trade is done and he retreats to settle accounts. Economic pressure is constant: defaults, delayed payments from city wholesalers, diesel-price hikes and the ever-present risk that a glut will leave him holding worthless stock.

topics.label: Family and Household
topics.profile: Venkatesh lives with his wife Vasantha, their two sons aged fourteen and ten, and his widowed mother in a modest tiled house on the edge of Bangarpet town. Vasantha manages the household and a small kitchen garden; she once worked as a school helper but left the job after their younger son was born. His elder son studies in ninth standard at the government high school in town; the younger is in fifth. Venkatesh's father, a small mango grower near Srinivaspur, died eight years ago, and the family orchard—three acres—was split between Venkatesh and his two brothers. He sold his share to fund the initial capital for the commission business. His mother helps with cooking and watches the boys when Vasantha visits her parents in Malur. Gender roles remain traditional: Vasantha handles all domestic work, while Venkatesh makes financial decisions and maintains external business relationships. The marriage was arranged within the Vokkaliga community eighteen years ago. Extended family gatherings happen at festival times—Ugadi, Deepavali—and at weddings, though the demands of the market mean he often arrives late or leaves early.

topics.label: Education and Schooling
topics.profile: Venkatesh himself studied up to second PUC in Bangarpet before his father called him home to help with mango harvests; he never enrolled in college, a fact he quietly regrets. Both his sons attend the government Kannada-medium high school in town. Fees are minimal, but textbooks, uniforms, and the elder boy's demand for a smartphone for online homework add up. The school is a fifteen-minute walk from home, crowded but functional; the headmaster is strict and SSLC results have been improving. Venkatesh hopes his elder son will finish PUC and get into a BCom course in Kolar or even Bengaluru, something he frames as 'a steady job path, not this daily tension.' The boy is a decent student, ranking in the top third of his class, but Venkatesh worries about the cost of private coaching if he aims for competitive exams. The younger son is more playful, less studious. Vasantha insists both boys will finish schooling no matter what; she has seen too many families pull children out for work. The family spends around ₹8,000 a year on education, counting everything. Venkatesh also quietly funds the school fees of a cousin's daughter in Srinivaspur whose father is a struggling dryland farmer.

topics.label: Health and Wellbeing
topics.profile: Venkatesh's mother has skeletal fluorosis—bowed legs, joint pain—from decades of drinking borewell water in Srinivaspur; she now relies on bottled water, but the damage is done. The family buys twenty-litre cans for drinking, though cooking and washing still use the municipal tap supply, which itself is borewell-fed and high in fluoride. Venkatesh himself suffers from chronic acidity and occasional chest pain, which he attributes to stress and the habit of skipping breakfast during peak market hours. He visited the government hospital in Kolar town twice last year for ECG tests; the doctor advised weight loss and less tension—easier said than done. Vasantha and the boys are generally healthy, though both children have dental mottling, an early sign of fluorosis. Healthcare for minor illnesses means the nearby private clinic; anything serious requires a trip to R.L. Jalappa Hospital in Tamaka or even Bengaluru. Venkatesh has no health insurance; a heart procedure or major surgery would mean selling assets or borrowing. He smokes five or six beedis a day—a habit he knows he should quit—and drinks occasionally with fellow traders. The fear of a sudden illness that stops him working, leaving the family without income, haunts him more than the market's daily ups and downs.

topics.label: Community and Belief
topics.profile: Venkatesh is Vokkaliga, the dominant landowning community in Kolar, though his family's small mango plot hardly makes them big farmers. Caste identity matters in business—most of his trusted contacts in the tomato trade are also Vokkaliga—and in marriage alliances. Social ties are dense: the weekly trade brings him into contact with hundreds of farmers, transporters and buyers, and reciprocal favours oil every transaction. He is a member of the Bangarpet Tomato Merchants' Association, which lobbies for better yard facilities and helps settle disputes. Religious life centres on the Someshwara temple in town; Venkatesh makes offerings during Shivaratri and before the start of the harvest season. His mother is more devout, visiting the temple weekly and observing fasts. The family also attends the annual jatre at Avani, an hour away. Venkatesh has heard of the Siddaganga Mutt's free hostels and wishes something similar existed closer by for poorer farmers' children. He contributes modestly to community functions—temple repairs, school prize days—and lends money interest-free within his extended family circle. Trust and reputation are everything in his trade; a broken promise can close doors across the district.

topics.label: Civic Life and Government
topics.profile: Venkatesh's direct dealings with government are limited but recurring. He has a GST registration for the commission business, which means monthly filings he outsources to a local accountant for ₹1,500 a year. The market yard itself is run by the APMC, and he has lobbied—unsuccessfully so far—for better drainage and a cold-storage facility to buffer price crashes. His wife uses the Shakti bus pass for trips to Malur and Kolar, saving the family a couple of hundred rupees a month. The KC-Valley treated-wastewater scheme has refilled some tanks near Bangarpet, bringing more tomato acreage under reliable irrigation—good for his trade, though farmers grumble about the water quality and the scheme's upkeep. Venkatesh himself has no land to benefit directly. He distrusts most politicians, viewing them as responsive only during election season, but respects local leaders who get roads repaired or transformers fixed. The Yettinahole project is a distant promise he has heard about for years; he will believe it when water actually flows. His main expectation from government is simpler: stable electricity, passable roads for lorries, and fair weighbridge practices at checkposts.

topics.label: Worldview and Concerns
topics.profile: Venkatesh is proud of his ability to read the market—when to hold, when to push a deal—and of keeping his sons in school despite the tomato trade's volatility. He worries most about a sudden price collapse that leaves him unable to recover advances given to farmers, a situation that has happened twice in the past five years and cost him a lakh each time. He blames the absence of proper cold storage and processing units for the worst of the price swings, and wishes government or private investors would build them. He resents big wholesale traders in Bengaluru who delay payments and squeeze his margins, but sees no alternative—that is where the demand is. Venkatesh also worries privately about his heart, his mother's worsening mobility, and the fluoride in every glass of water his children drink. He demands better: a functional APMC cold chain, insurance schemes that actually cover small traders, reliable treated water or a piped Cauvery supply to replace the failing borewells, and schools with enough teachers so his sons do not need expensive private tuition. What keeps him going is the hope that the next season will be kinder, and the belief that education will lift his sons out of the daily price lottery that defines his own life.
